additional_requirements: Functioning is not markedly impaired apart from the impact of the delusion(s) or its ramifications

S019.name: Delusions
S019.description: Fixed beliefs that do not change easily, even in the face of contradictory evidence.

subtypes.Persecutory Delusions: The false belief that one is being harmed or monitored by other people or organizations.
subtypes.Referential Delusions: The conviction that ordinary events, remarks, or behaviors have specific relevance to oneself.
subtypes.Grandiose Delusions: The false belief that one possesses special abilities, power, or fame.
subtypes.Erotomanic Delusions: The false belief that another person is in love with or has affection for them.
subtypes.Nihilistic Delusions: A destructive or negative conviction that the world is ending or that a major catastrophe will occur.
subtypes.Somatic Delusions: The baseless conviction that there is a serious abnormality with one's body or organs.
subtypes.Jealous Delusions: The conviction that one's spouse or romantic partner is being unfaithful without sufficient evidence.

symptom.disease_info: Delusional disorder is characterized by the presence of one or more persistent, non-bizarre or minimally bizarre delusions lasting at least one month in a person whose overall functioning is relatively preserved and whose behavior is not obviously odd or markedly disorganized outside the delusional context. Aside from the delusional beliefs, mood and thought processes are often relatively intact, and criteria for schizophrenia (such as prominent hallucinations, disorganized speech, or negative symptoms) are not met. Onset is typically in mid to late adulthood and may be associated with psychosocial stressors, social isolation, sensory impairment, or personality traits such as suspiciousness or rigidity. The course is usually chronic, with beliefs that remain fixed despite clear contradictory evidence, and individuals may only come to clinical attention when interpersonal conflict, legal problems, or functional decline arise directly from their delusional convictions.

patient.personality: Ulisses is a socially engaged, organized, and ambitious student-leader who thrives on coordinating events, helping his community, and staying deeply involved with friends and soccer.
patient.stressor: In his first year of college, Ulisses threw himself into campus leadership, community activism, and coordinating local soccer tournaments while juggling classes and commuting from home, leaving little downtime and mounting pressure to perform. After a contentious student election and a dispute over field permits for a tournament he helped organize, he felt unfairly blamed and began replaying email threads and group chats, convinced that certain peers were working against him behind the scenes. Over the following months, he became increasingly preoccupied with interpreting routine scheduling changes, social media posts, and minor setbacks as part of a coordinated effort, even as he maintained his grades and continued volunteering. Friends and a trusted faculty advisor, worried by how rigidly he held to this specific narrative despite reassurances and evidence to the contrary, encouraged him to see a mental health professional when organizing even small events started to revolve around his attempts to anticipate and counter these perceived machinations.
patient.chief_complaint: “I keep getting stuck on certain ideas about what people are really doing, and no matter what anyone says, I can’t shake these beliefs.”

S019.name: Delusions
S019.description: Fixed beliefs that do not change easily, even in the face of contradictory evidence.
S019.manifestation: Ever since that whole mess with the election and the field permits, I’ve been convinced that a specific group of students is quietly coordinating things like meeting times, room changes, and even vague posts on Instagram to undermine anything I try to organize, and even when people show me it’s just a coincidence, it still feels absolutely clear to me that they’re doing it on purpose.
